questions.title: Lung carcinoma and the lingula
questions.question: A 75-year-old woman was admitted to hospital, and bronchograms and radiographs revealed a lung carcinoma in her left lung. Which of the following structures or characteristics does the cancerous (left) lung contain?

options.B: Groove for the superior vena cava

explanations.A: Incorrect. Both lungs have an oblique fissure, but the transverse (horizontal) fissure is unique to the right lung, where it separates the upper from the middle lobe — the left lung has no horizontal fissure at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior vena caval groove is an impression on the mediastinal surface of the right lung, related to the right atrium's venous drainage, not a feature of the left lung.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A middle lobe exists only on the right lung, produced by its unique horizontal fissure. The left lung has only an upper and lower lobe.
explanations.D: Correct. The lingula is a tongue-shaped extension of the left lung's upper lobe, lying below the cardiac notch on the anterior border — it occupies the same anatomical territory the middle lobe occupies on the right, but without being a separate lobe. It is the single most reliable answer among these options for any question asking what the left (rather than right) lung specifically contains, since a transverse fissure, an SVC groove and a middle lobe are all right-lung-only features.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the lingula as the feature unique to the left lung among right-lung-only distractors (transverse fissure, SVC groove, middle lobe).

questions.title: Ligation for inferior thyroid artery bleeding
questions.question: During surgery on a 56-year-old man for a squamous cell carcinoma of the neck, a surgeon notices profuse bleeding from the inferior thyroid artery. Which of the following arteries must be ligated immediately to stop the bleeding?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The transverse cervical artery is itself a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, not its parent vessel — ligating it alone would not achieve proximal control of the trunk that also supplies the bleeding inferior thyroid artery.
explanations.B: Correct. The inferior thyroid artery is short and retracts into the deep neck once torn, so proximal control of profuse bleeding from it is achieved by ligating its parent vessel, the thyrocervical trunk, a short branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. This trunk also gives the transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries, but it is its relationship to the inferior thyroid artery that makes it the vessel to ligate here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The costocervical trunk is a separate branch of the subclavian artery, supplying the superior intercostal and deep cervical territory — it has no relationship to the inferior thyroid artery or thyroid bleeding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ascending cervical artery is a small branch of the inferior thyroid artery itself, too distal and too small to provide proximal control of the bleeding.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the thyrocervical trunk is ligated for proximal control of inferior thyroid artery bleeding.

questions.title: Recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion and the thyroarytenoid
questions.question: A 26-year-old singer visits her ENT physician complaining of changes in her voice. A laryngoscopic examination demonstrates a lesion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing weakness of which of the following muscles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cricothyroid is the one intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve — it would be spared, not weakened, by a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior constrictor is a pharyngeal muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via the pharyngeal branch), not the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid, including the thyroarytenoid — a lesion of the nerve therefore weakens the thyroarytenoid, producing the hoarseness and voice change this patient presents with. This is why laryngeal-nerve palsies are grouped by which muscles they spare rather than which they weaken — cricothyroid sparing is the diagnostic clue that localises the lesion to the recurrent, not the external, laryngeal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The middle constrictor, like the superior constrictor, is a pharyngeal muscle supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, not an intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the thyroarytenoid as one of the muscles weakened by a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion, since the nerve supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except cricothyroid.

questions.title: Sphenoethmoidal recess swelling
questions.question: A 53-year-old man has difficulty breathing through his nose. On examination, his physician finds swelling of the mucous membranes of the sphenoethmoidal recess. Which opening of the paranasal sinuses is most likely plugged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The middle ethmoidal cells drain into the middle meatus, not the sphenoethmoidal recess.
explanations.B: Correct. The sphenoethmoidal recess is a narrow space in the roof of the nasal cavity into which the sphenoid sinus alone drains, so swelling confined to this recess plugs the sphenoid sinus specifically. The middle and superior meatus, by contrast, each drain a different named group of sinuses, so identifying which meatus or recess is inflamed is what actually localises the affected sinus on examination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus, a distinct opening from the sphenoethmoidal recess, even though both are in the posterior nasal roof region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal cells drain into the middle meatus, along with the frontal and maxillary sinuses — none of these use the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name the sphenoid sinus as the paranasal sinus draining through the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.title: Foreign body aspiration in a child
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy develops sudden cyanosis and dyspnea. During bronchoscopy, where is an inhaled foreign body most likely to be lodged, causing this obstruction?

explanations.A: Correct. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertically oriented — a straighter continuation of the trachea's axis — than the left, which is longer and more oblique because it passes beneath the aortic arch. An inhaled foreign body follows the path of least resistance and lodges in the right main bronchus far more often than the left, in both children and adults.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left main bronchus is the less likely site precisely because of its greater length and obliquity, crossing beneath the aortic arch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A lobar bronchus is a smaller-calibre branch beyond the main bronchus; a foreign body typically lodges more proximally, in the wider right main bronchus itself, before reaching a lobar branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although the right side is favoured, the obstruction is described as occurring at the main bronchus, the widest and most direct pathway, not at the narrower superior lobar branch.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that an inhaled foreign body most often lodges in the right main bronchus and explain why.

questions.title: Thoracic duct injury and chylothorax
questions.question: A 28-year-old man presented with severe trauma, and the thoracic duct was accidentally damaged during assessment. The resulting accumulation of lymph in the pleural cavity is referred to as which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pleurisy names inflammation of the pleura; it does not specify a particular fluid type collecting in the pleural cavity.
explanations.B: Correct. Chylothorax is lymph (chyle, the fat-rich lymph the thoracic duct carries) accumulating in the pleural cavity, which is exactly what results when the thoracic duct — running through the thorax alongside the oesophagus and aorta before draining into the left venous angle — is torn. Recognising chylothorax specifically (rather than a generic traumatic effusion) matters clinically, since chyle drainage carries different nutritional and management implications from blood, pus or simple inflammatory fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphedema is lymph accumulating in the tissues (typically a limb), not in a body cavity such as the pleural space.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyothorax (empyema) is pus in the pleural cavity, arising from infection, not from lymphatic duct injury.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name chylothorax as lymph accumulation in the pleural cavity following thoracic duct injury.

questions.title: Feature of the laryngopharynx
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of the laryngopharynx?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil) is a feature of the nasopharynx, not the laryngopharynx.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tubal tonsil surrounds the opening of the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube in the nasopharynx, not the laryngopharynx.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The palatine tonsils sit in the tonsillar fossae of the oropharynx, a different part of the pharynx from the laryngopharynx.
explanations.D: Correct. The piriform recess (fossa) is a mucosal gutter on each side of the laryngeal inlet, specifically a feature of the laryngopharynx (hypopharynx) — and the site where a swallowed foreign body most often lodges. This distinguishes it from the nasopharynx's adenoid and tubal tonsil and the oropharynx's palatine tonsils, each of which marks a different part of the pharynx rather than the laryngopharynx.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the piriform recess as a feature of the laryngopharynx, distinct from the nasopharynx and oropharynx's own named features.

questions.title: Inability to abduct the vocal cords
questions.question: A young singer visits her physician complaining of vocal difficulties. On examination, she is unable to abduct the vocal cords during quiet breathing. Which of the following muscles is most likely paralyzed?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vocalis (part of the thyroarytenoid) shortens and relaxes the vocal fold rather than abducting it, so its paralysis would not remove abduction specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cricothyroid tenses (lengthens) the vocal folds to raise pitch — it plays no role in abduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oblique arytenoid, along with the transverse arytenoid, adducts the vocal folds (closing the airway), the opposite action to abduction.
explanations.D: Correct. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds, rotating the arytenoid cartilage to swing the vocal process laterally and open the airway — its paralysis removes the only muscle capable of abduction, explaining this patient's inability to abduct her vocal cords. The lateral cricoarytenoid and interarytenoid muscles adduct the folds instead, and the cricothyroid only tenses them, so none of those muscles could produce a pure loss of abduction on its own.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds.

questions.title: Epistaxis from Little's area
questions.question: A 20-year-old man enters the emergency room with bleeding from his right nostril. On examination he looks well. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals bleeding from the anterior part of the nasal septum, corresponding to Little's area. Which of the following arteries is the main source of the bleeding?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior labial artery is one of the smaller contributors to Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), not the dominant source of bleeding from it.
explanations.B: Correct. The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, is the dominant contributor to the anastomotic plexus at Little's area and the leading source of anterior epistaxis originating there. Its anastomotic partners — the anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial arteries — also supply the plexus, but none contributes as much to bleeding from this site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lesser palatine artery is also a minor contributor to the plexus, not its dominant vessel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal artery contributes to Little's area from above, but is not the dominant source — the sphenopalatine artery's contribution is larger and clinically more significant.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name the sphenopalatine artery as the main source of bleeding from Little's area among its anastomotic partners.

questions.title: Carotid buffer nerve stimulation
questions.question: Regarding the buffer (baroreceptor) nerves of the carotid sinus, which one of the following occurs with their stimulation?

options.A: Excitatory impulses to the vasomotor centre
options.D: Excitatory impulses to the cardio-stimulatory centre

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rising carotid sinus pressure increases afferent firing along the buffer nerve, which inhibits, rather than excites, the vasomotor centre.
explanations.B: Correct. Stimulation of the carotid buffer nerve inhibits sympathetic vasomotor and cardio-stimulatory outflow while raising vagal tone, producing reflex hypotension and bradycardia — the buffering response that opposes a rise in arterial pressure. This reflex is the mechanism by which carotid sinus massage can slow the heart therapeutically in certain arrhythmias, and reversing its direction is the classic distractor for this question.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes the opposite of the buffer nerve's actual effect; hypertension and tachycardia would result from reduced, not increased, baroreceptor afferent activity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The buffer nerve's signal inhibits the cardio-stimulatory centre, not excites it — reversing this direction is the classic distractor for this reflex.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that carotid buffer nerve stimulation produces reflex hypotension and bradycardia via central inhibition.

questions.title: Mechanism of neurogenic shock
questions.question: Which of the following best describes neurogenic shock?

options.C: Vasodilation of skeletal muscle blood vessels
options.D: Stimulation of the vasomotor centre by bacterial endotoxins

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vasoconstriction of arterioles describes the body's compensatory sympathetic response in hypovolaemic shock, the opposite of neurogenic shock's loss-of-tone mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neurogenic shock is caused by a sudden loss, not an increase, of sympathetic outflow to blood vessels.
explanations.C: Correct. Neurogenic shock follows sudden loss of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone — typically from high spinal cord injury or deep anaesthesia — leaving skeletal muscle and other peripheral vascular beds unopposed and widely dilated, pooling blood peripherally and dropping venous return and cardiac output. This loss-of-tone mechanism is the opposite of the compensatory vasoconstriction and increased sympathetic activity the body mounts in hypovolaemic shock, and a different trigger from septic shock's endotoxin-driven vasomotor centre stimulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stimulation of the vasomotor centre by bacterial endotoxins describes the mechanism of septic shock, a different trigger from neurogenic shock's loss of sympathetic tone.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Describe neurogenic shock as skeletal-muscle vasodilation from loss of sympathetic vascular tone.

questions.title: Heart sound at isometric relaxation
questions.question: During the isometric relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle, which one of the following is heard?

explanations.A: Correct. Isometric (isovolumetric) relaxation is the phase immediately after ventricular ejection, when the semilunar valves close while the AV valves remain shut; the second heart sound (S2), generated by semilunar valve closure, marks the very start of this phase. This distinguishes it from the first heart sound (S1, AV valve closure at the start of isometric contraction), the third (rapid ventricular filling) and the fourth (atrial contraction), each of which marks a different point in the cycle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The first heart sound (S1) is generated by AV valve closure at the start of isometric contraction, the opposite end of systole from isometric relaxation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third heart sound (S3), when present, occurs during rapid ventricular filling, later in diastole than isometric relaxation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fourth heart sound (S4), when present, occurs with atrial contraction, at the very end of diastole, not at isometric relaxation.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that the second heart sound marks the onset of isometric relaxation.

questions.title: Plasma volume restoration after haemorrhage
questions.question: 24 hours after haemorrhage, which of the following mechanisms causes restoration of plasma volume?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiotensin II secretion increases, not decreases, after haemorrhage, as part of the renin-angiotensin system's response to falling pressure — and its contribution to volume restoration is renal and slower than the capillary shift.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Venous dilation would reduce, not restore, effective circulating volume by increasing venous capacitance.
explanations.C: Correct. Falling capillary hydrostatic pressure after haemorrhage shifts the Starling balance so interstitial fluid moves back into the vascular space — the capillary shift mechanism — restoring plasma volume within roughly 24 to 48 hours, ahead of the slower renal and endocrine contributions. This mechanism explains why a haemorrhage patient's haematocrit can look artificially low on the following day, since plasma volume is restored well before the lost red cell mass is replaced.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thirst sensation increases, not decreases, after haemorrhage (partly via angiotensin II), promoting water intake to help restore volume.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: Name the capillary shift mechanism as the process restoring plasma volume in the first 24 hours after haemorrhage.

questions.title: Effect of angiotensin II
questions.question: The renin-angiotensin system has a vital role in regulating arterial blood pressure. What is the effect of angiotensin II?

options.A: Has a strong direct arteriolar vasodilator effect
options.B: Inhibits noradrenaline release from postganglionic sympathetic neurons
options.C: Stimulates thirst sensation, which increases water intake
options.D: Inhibits antidiuretic hormone secretion from the posterior pituitary

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiotensin II is a potent direct arteriolar vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator — this option reverses its actual effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Angiotensin II facilitates (increases), rather than inhibits, noradrenaline release from postganglionic sympathetic neurons, reinforcing sympathetic vasoconstriction.
explanations.C: Correct. Angiotensin II stimulates the hypothalamic thirst centre, increasing water intake, as one of several coordinated actions that raise arterial pressure and conserve circulating volume. Its other actions — direct arteriolar vasoconstriction, facilitated noradrenaline release and stimulated ADH secretion — are all likewise pressure-raising or volume-conserving, never the reverse.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin II stimulates, rather than inhibits, ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary, promoting water retention rather than diuresis.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that angiotensin II stimulates thirst as one of its several pressure-raising, volume-conserving actions.

questions.title: Cause of death in refractory shock
questions.question: What is the cause of death in refractory shock?

options.D: Release of toxins by ischemic tissues

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic respiratory failure is not the mechanism of death in refractory shock, which is an acute circulatory event, not a chronic pulmonary one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Refractory shock produces metabolic acidosis, from anaerobic metabolism in poorly perfused tissue, not alkalosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal plasma flow falls, not rises, in shock, as part of the generalised hypoperfusion.
explanations.D: Correct. In late, refractory shock, prolonged ischemia damages tissues that then release toxins (including vasoactive and myocardial-depressant substances) into the circulation — this systemic toxin release is the mechanism most directly implicated in death at this stage, once the shock state has become unresponsive to the usual compensatory and therapeutic measures. This distinguishes refractory shock's terminal mechanism from earlier, still-compensated stages of shock, where the circulation can still respond to fluid and vasopressor support.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that release of toxins by ischemic tissue is the cause of death in refractory shock.

questions.title: Hydrostatic indifferent point
questions.question: Regarding the hydrostatic indifferent point, which one of the following best describes it?

options.A: The pressure at its level is zero
options.B: It is shifted downward during swimming
options.C: It moves downward if the capacity of the leg veins decreases
options.D: It is normally 5-7 cm below the diaphragm

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hydrostatic indifferent point is where venous pressure does not change with posture, not where pressure is zero.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Swimming (immersion) shifts the point, but the described direction here does not match the expected shift during immersion, which is why this option is not the best answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reduced leg-vein capacity shifts the indifferent point downward, but the paper's key names the point's normal resting location, not this specific perturbation, as the single best description of the term.
explanations.D: Correct. The hydrostatic indifferent point — the venous level at which pressure is posture-independent — sits normally about 5 to 7 cm below the level of the diaphragm. This level is not fixed in every circumstance — it moves downward when leg-vein capacity falls, and shifts during immersion such as swimming, but the resting reference value given here is the one this question tests.

questions.subject: cvs
questions.learning_objective: State that the hydrostatic indifferent point sits normally 5-7 cm below the diaphragm.

questions.title: Conducting zone of the respiratory system
questions.question: Regarding the conducting zone of the respiratory system, which of the following statements is appropriate?

options.D: It contains the cells secreting surfactant

explanations.A: Incorrect. The conducting zone (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles) carries no alveoli — alveoli belong to the respiratory zone, where gas exchange occurs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 500 ml is roughly a typical tidal volume, not the conducting zone's own volume, which is normally about 150 ml.
explanations.C: Correct. Air occupying the conducting zone at end-inspiration takes no part in gas exchange; this volume is what the conducting zone is called — the anatomical dead space. This distinguishes the conducting zone from the alveoli-bearing respiratory zone, where gas exchange actually occurs, and from tidal volume, of which dead space is only a fraction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Surfactant-secreting cells (type II pneumocytes) line the alveoli of the respiratory zone, not the conducting airways.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the conducting zone is called the anatomical dead space.

questions.title: Muscle of quiet inspiration
questions.question: Which of the following is the most important muscle in producing the increase in thoracic volume during quiet, normal inspiration?

explanations.A: Correct. During quiet inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and descends, increasing thoracic volume mainly in its vertical dimension, and does the great majority of the work of breathing — the single most important muscle for this increase in thoracic volume. The external intercostals make only a smaller, accessory contribution, and the sternomastoid, scalene and abdominal muscles are recruited only during forced, not quiet, breathing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The abdominal muscles are expiratory muscles, recruited during forced (not quiet) expiration, not inspiration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sternomastoid is an accessory muscle recruited only during forced inspiration, not during quiet, resting breathing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal intercostal muscles assist forced expiration, not inspiration — the external intercostals, not internal, make the (smaller, accessory) inspiratory contribution.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name the diaphragm as the chief muscle of quiet inspiration.

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn-ink key, corrupted glyph on option a, confirmed by render --force (coverage/ZU-MED-106-triage.md)

questions.title: Muscles of forced expiration
questions.question: During forced expiration, which of the following respiratory muscles become contracted?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sternomastoid is an inspiratory accessory muscle, not an expiratory one — it is not recruited for forced expiration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external intercostals are inspiratory muscles; forced expiration recruits the internal, not external, intercostals.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The diaphragm is exclusively inspiratory and relaxes, rather than contracts, during any expiration, forced or quiet.
explanations.D: Correct. Forced (active) expiration recruits the internal intercostal muscles, which pull the ribs down and in, together with the abdominal muscles, which push the diaphragm upward and further compress the thoracic cavity. The diaphragm and external intercostals remain inspiratory muscles throughout and take no part in expiration, forced or otherwise.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles as the ones contracted during forced expiration.

questions.title: Prevention of pulmonary edema
questions.question: Pulmonary edema is prevented by decreasing which of the following?

options.A: Surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli

explanations.A: Correct. Surfactant lowers the surface tension of the fluid film lining each alveolus; it is specifically this reduction in surface tension that keeps pulmonary edema from developing, by preventing the alveolus from drawing fluid in from the capillaries. This is why surfactant deficiency, as in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, raises alveolar surface tension and predisposes to fluid accumulation — the same mechanism demonstrated in reverse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bronchial mucous secretion serves airway humidification and particle trapping, not the alveolar Starling-balance mechanism that governs pulmonary edema.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alveolar macrophage activity serves immune defence and particle clearance, unrelated to the surface-tension mechanism that prevents fluid accumulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ciliary escalator activity clears mucus and particles from the airway, a separate function from the alveolar fluid balance that surface tension governs.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that decreasing alveolar surface tension (via surfactant) prevents pulmonary edema.

questions.title: Definition of hypoxia
questions.question: Which of the following statements defines hypoxia?

options.C: Diminished O2 supply at the tissue level
options.D: Bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dyspnea on lying down describes orthopnea, a symptom that can accompany certain cardiopulmonary conditions, not the definition of hypoxia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Awareness of breathing is closer to a description of dyspnea in general, not hypoxia's definition.
explanations.C: Correct. Hypoxia is defined as diminished oxygen supply at the tissue level, regardless of the underlying mechanism (hypoxic, anaemic, stagnant or histotoxic hypoxia are all subtypes of this one definition). Cyanosis, by contrast, is only a possible accompanying sign of hypoxia — it can be absent even in severe hypoxia, such as severe anaemia, where there is too little haemoglobin overall to show the discoloration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cyanosis (bluish discoloration) is only a possible accompanying sign of hypoxia, not its definition — it can be absent even in significant hypoxia, such as severe anaemic hypoxia, where there is too little haemoglobin overall to show the discoloration.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Define hypoxia as diminished oxygen supply at the tissue level, distinct from cyanosis.

questions.title: Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle
questions.question: As regards bronchial tone, which factor can relax the bronchial smooth muscle?

explanations.A: Correct. Vasoactive intestinal peptide (V.I.P.), released from non-adrenergic non-cholinergic nerve fibres in the airway, is a relaxant of bronchial smooth muscle, reducing bronchial tone. This is the opposite effect to histamine, leukotrienes and irritant stimuli, all of which constrict bronchial smooth muscle and raise airway resistance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Histamine constricts, rather than relaxes, bronchial smooth muscle, raising airway resistance as an inflammatory mediator.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leukotrienes, like histamine, are bronchoconstrictor inflammatory mediators, not relaxants.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Irritant stimuli trigger reflex bronchoconstriction, the opposite effect to relaxation.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name V.I.P. as a relaxant of bronchial smooth muscle, distinguishing it from constrictor mediators.

questions.title: Hypoxia from decreased blood supply
questions.question: When the blood supply to a tissue decreases, what type of hypoxia occurs?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histotoxic hypoxia results from a tissue's inability to use available oxygen (e.g. cyanide poisoning), not from reduced blood supply.
explanations.B: Correct. Stagnant hypoxia results from decreased blood supply (flow) to a tissue, whether generalized (as in shock) or localized (as in arterial or venous obstruction) — the oxygen content of the blood may be normal, but too little of it reaches the tissue. This is distinct from hypoxic hypoxia (low arterial PO2), anaemic hypoxia (reduced oxygen-carrying capacity) and histotoxic hypoxia (inability to use available oxygen), each with a different underlying defect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypoxic hypoxia results from a low arterial PO2 (e.g. at altitude or with lung disease), a different mechanism from reduced blood flow with normal oxygen content.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Anaemic hypoxia results from reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood (low haemoglobin), not from reduced blood flow.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Name stagnant hypoxia as the type caused by decreased blood supply to a tissue.

questions.title: Central chemoreceptor sensitivity
questions.question: The central chemoreceptors are more sensitive to which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Central chemoreceptors are not directly sensitive to arterial O2 lack — that is the peripheral chemoreceptors' domain, activated sharply once PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg.
explanations.B: Correct. Central chemoreceptors near the medulla, protected by the blood-brain barrier and bathed by CSF, respond mainly to rising PCO2 (via the CSF H+ it generates once CO2, not H+ itself, crosses the blood-brain barrier), providing the majority (about 75-80%) of resting respiratory drive. Peripheral chemoreceptors, by contrast, monitor arterial PO2 directly and contribute the remaining 20-25% of resting drive, switching on sharply only once PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg.
explanations.C: Incorrect. K+ excess is not the stimulus central chemoreceptors are described as being most sensitive to in this context.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alkalinity (a rise in pH) would reduce, not increase, chemoreceptor drive — the reverse of the acidifying effect of CO2 excess that actually stimulates them.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to CO2 excess (via CSF H+), not O2 lack.

questions.title: LDL receptor specificity
questions.question: The LDL receptor is specific for which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Apo A is the major apolipoprotein of HDL, not a ligand the LDL receptor recognises.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Apo D is not one of the apolipoproteins the LDL receptor is specific for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Apo B48 is the intestinal, chylomicron form of apo B, which lacks the LDL receptor-binding domain — chylomicron remnants are cleared via apo E, not apo B48.
explanations.D: Correct. The LDL receptor recognises lipoproteins carrying apolipoprotein B100 (on LDL particles) or apolipoprotein E (on remnant/IDL particles), mediating their receptor-mediated endocytosis. It does not bind apo A (HDL's major apolipoprotein), apo D, or apo B48 alone, the intestinal chylomicron form of apo B that lacks the receptor-binding domain.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the LDL receptor is specific for apo B100 and apo E.

questions.title: Committed step of cholesterol biosynthesis
questions.question: What is the committed step in the biosynthesis of cholesterol from acetyl CoA?

options.A: Formation of acetoacetyl CoA from acetyl CoA
options.B: Formation of mevalonate from HMG CoA
options.C: Formation of HMG CoA from acetyl CoA and acetoacetyl CoA
options.D: Formation of squalene by squalene synthetase

explanations.A: Incorrect. Formation of acetoacetyl CoA is an early, reversible step shared with ketone body metabolism, not the committed step.
explanations.B: Correct. The conversion of HMG CoA to mevalonate, catalysed by the rate-limiting, statin-targeted enzyme HMG CoA reductase, is the pathway's committed, irreversible step. The earlier steps — acetoacetyl CoA and HMG CoA formation — are reversible and shared with ketone body metabolism, and squalene formation happens well after the pathway is already committed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Formation of HMG CoA is also an earlier, reversible step, occurring before the pathway is committed to cholesterol synthesis specifically.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Squalene formation occurs later in the pathway, well after the committing reductase step has already taken place.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name mevalonate formation from HMG CoA as cholesterol biosynthesis's committed step.

questions.title: Apolipoprotein CII activation
questions.question: Apolipoprotein CII acts as an activator of which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Apolipoprotein CII, carried on chylomicrons and VLDL, is the obligatory activator of lipoprotein lipase, the endothelial enzyme that hydrolyses these particles' triglyceride core to release free fatty acids. This is distinct from apo A-I's role activating LCAT for cholesterol esterification in HDL, a different apolipoprotein-enzyme pairing entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LCAT is activated by apo A-I, not apo CII, and esterifies cholesterol within HDL, a different enzyme and substrate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phospholipase C is a signalling enzyme unrelated to lipoprotein metabolism or apo CII's activating role.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ACAT esterifies cholesterol intracellularly and is not activated by apo CII.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name lipoprotein lipase as the enzyme apolipoprotein CII activates.

questions.title: NADPH source for fatty acid synthesis
questions.question: The majority of the NADPH used during the synthesis of fatty acids is derived from which of the following?

options.D: The mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase enzyme reaction

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glycolysis generates NADH, not NADPH — the two reduced cofactors serve different metabolic roles and are not interchangeable in this context.
explanations.B: Correct. The hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) pathway is the major source of NADPH in lipogenic tissues, generating it through the oxidative reactions catalysed by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase. Glycolysis, by contrast, generates NADH rather than NADPH, so it is never the correct answer to a question asking specifically about the NADPH supply for lipogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The citrate lyase/malic enzyme shuttle contributes some NADPH, but is a minor contributor compared with the HMP pathway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase is not the majority NADPH source for cytoplasmic fatty acid synthesis; the HMP pathway's contribution is larger.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name the hexose monophosphate pathway as the majority NADPH source for fatty acid synthesis.

questions.title: De novo fatty acid synthesis
questions.question: De novo synthesis of fatty acids is one of the sources of fatty acid. Which of the following is true about the de novo synthesis of fatty acids?

options.B: Malonyl CoA is the direct source of all carbon atoms needed
options.C: Fatty acid synthase is the key enzyme

explanations.A: Incorrect. De novo fatty acid synthesis is a cytoplasmic pathway; mitochondria is where the reverse process, beta-oxidation, takes place.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malonyl CoA donates two-carbon units for chain elongation, but the acetyl CoA primer also contributes carbons — malonyl CoA is not literally the source of every carbon atom in the final product.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer here. Fatty acid synthase is genuinely the multi-enzyme complex that catalyses the pathway, but the printed key on this exam paper names the NADPH+H+ requirement as the intended single best answer; the cofactor requirement is an absolute, unconditional stoichiometric fact about every elongation cycle, while naming 'the key enzyme' is a broader, less specific description of the same pathway.
explanations.D: Correct. Every two-carbon addition cycle in fatty acid synthesis consumes NADPH+H+ as the reducing power for its two reduction steps (beta-ketoacyl reduction and enoyl reduction) — an absolute requirement of the pathway, and the answer the paper's own printed key selects. The pathway itself is cytoplasmic, not mitochondrial, and uses malonyl CoA as the two-carbon donor for chain elongation, with fatty acid synthase as the enzyme complex carrying out the reaction.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that de novo fatty acid synthesis requires NADPH+H+ at each elongation cycle, and is a cytoplasmic pathway using malonyl CoA as chain-elongation donor.

questions.title: Enzyme deficiency in Tay-Sachs disease
questions.question: Tay-Sachs disease is due to a defect of which of the following enzymes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, a different sphingolipidosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, not Tay-Sachs.
explanations.C: Correct. Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of hexosaminidase A, the enzyme that normally degrades GM2 ganglioside, which then accumulates progressively in neurons, causing severe neurodegeneration. This distinguishes Tay-Sachs from the other classic sphingolipidoses — Niemann-Pick (sphingomyelinase), Krabbe (galactocerebrosidase) and Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase) disease — each defined by its own specific enzyme deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, a different sphingolipidosis from Tay-Sachs.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name hexosaminidase A deficiency as the cause of Tay-Sachs disease.

questions.title: Thymic epithelial reticular cells
questions.question: The epithelial reticular cells of the thymus gland have which of the following criteria?

options.A: They are concerned with reticular fibre synthesis
options.B: They are derived from embryonic mesoderm
options.C: They are joined together by cell junctions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thymic epithelial reticular cells produce no reticular fibres — a key feature distinguishing them from the true reticular cells of other lymphoid organs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thymic epithelial reticular cells are endodermal in origin, not mesodermal.
explanations.C: Correct. Thymic epithelial reticular cells are joined together by cell junctions (desmosomes), forming a cellular reticulum that supports developing thymocytes, rather than being held together by a true reticular fibre network. They are also endodermal in origin and produce no reticular fibres themselves, distinguishing them from the true reticular cells of other lymphoid organs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thymic epithelial reticular cells are typically described with long, branching (stellate) processes, not short, wide ones.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: State that thymic epithelial reticular cells are joined by cell junctions, endodermal, and produce no reticular fibres.

questions.title: Splenic sinusoid characteristics
questions.question: The splenic sinusoid is characterized by which of the following?

options.A: It is located in the white pulp
options.C: It has a continuous basement membrane
options.D: Tight junctions are present between its endothelial cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Splenic sinusoids are located in the red pulp, not the white pulp.
explanations.B: Correct. Splenic sinusoids are lined by elongated (rod-shaped) endothelial cells arranged with slit-like gaps between them, an arrangement central to the open/closed-theory debate over how blood crosses from the terminal capillaries into the sinusoids. Their discontinuous basement membrane and the absence of tight junctions between them together permit blood cells to filter through the sinusoidal wall, the spleen's characteristic filtering function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The splenic sinusoid basement membrane is discontinuous (annular/ring-like), not continuous — this discontinuity is part of what allows blood cells to pass through the sinusoidal wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The gaps between splenic sinusoidal endothelial cells are not sealed by tight junctions; this open arrangement is what permits the sinusoid's filtering function.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: State that splenic sinusoid endothelial cells are elongated, in the red pulp, with a discontinuous basement membrane.

questions.title: Basilar artery characteristics
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes the basilar artery?

options.C: Has a wide lumen and thin wall
options.D: Has many valves within its wall

explanations.A: Incorrect. The basilar artery, like other muscular arteries, possesses an internal elastic lamina — it does not lack one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The basilar artery's adventitia is thin, not thick, consistent with its overall thin-walled histological character.
explanations.C: Correct. The basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries and supplying the brainstem and posterior brain, is histologically characterised — like other large cerebral arteries — by a wide lumen and a comparatively thin wall. It nonetheless possesses an internal elastic lamina, like other muscular arteries, and a thin rather than thick adventitia — occlusion of this vessel causes a distinct, high-mortality brainstem stroke syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteries in general, including the basilar artery, do not contain valves — valves are a feature of veins, not arteries.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: State that the basilar artery is characterised by a wide lumen and thin wall.

questions.title: Blood capillaries within nervous tissue
questions.question: Which of the following characterizes blood capillaries within the nervous tissue?

options.A: Contain pinocytic vesicles that permit transport
options.C: Have large pores within the endothelial cells
options.D: Are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium

explanations.A: Correct. Capillaries within nervous tissue are continuous capillaries with a tight, unfenestrated endothelium — the structural basis of the blood-brain barrier — so transport across them relies on pinocytic (transcytotic) vesicles rather than pores. This continuous, tightly-sealed endothelium is why many drugs effective against peripheral disease cannot reach therapeutic concentrations in the central nervous system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nervous-tissue capillaries have a complete, not incomplete, basal lamina, part of the tight seal that forms the blood-brain barrier.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nervous-tissue capillaries have no large pores — that describes fenestrated capillaries found elsewhere in the body, not the continuous capillaries of the blood-brain barrier.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Capillary endothelium, in nervous tissue as everywhere else in the body, is simple squamous, never simple cuboidal.

questions.subject: haem
questions.learning_objective: State that nervous-tissue capillaries transport material via pinocytic vesicles, consistent with their continuous, tight-junctioned endothelium.

questions.title: Character of the terminal bronchiole
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of the terminal bronchiole?

options.A: Lined by ciliated cells and goblet cells
options.B: Its lamina propria has no glands

explanations.A: Incorrect. The terminal bronchiole is lined by ciliated cells and Clara (club) cells, but goblet cells are absent from bronchioles generally, having disappeared more proximally in the airway.
explanations.B: Correct. The terminal bronchiole's lamina propria contains no glands, distinguishing its wall from the larger bronchi, whose submucosa carries seromucous glands. This absence of glands, together with the absence of cartilage and goblet cells, marks the terminal bronchiole as structurally simpler than the larger, cartilage- and gland-bearing bronchi proximal to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cartilage is absent from bronchiole walls entirely, including the terminal bronchiole — cartilage is a feature of the bronchi, not the bronchioles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the respiratory bronchiole, not the terminal bronchiole, whose wall is interrupted by scattered alveoli — the terminal bronchiole itself carries no alveoli.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the terminal bronchiole's lamina propria carries no glands, distinct from the larger bronchi.
